A PLACE CALLED HOPE

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a Place Called Hope, the last safe haven for foreign nationals affected by xenophobia now also under threat.

Summary:
When xenophobic attacks flared up in April in parts of KZN thousand of foreign nationals were displaced. Many to shelter in temporary refugee camps set up local municipalities. But three months later, those camps would be torn down leaving many of the foreigners displaced again.
A family in Camperdown opened their doors, welcoming the refugees to Hope Farm. But just one month later, the owners are now being threatened with legal action against them if they do not remove the people from their privately owned farm.

We bring you the stories of a community desperate for a place to call home, a family that wanted to help and municipality that is out to get them.


Further information:
“When people ask us why we did what we did, my response is: ‘How could we not?’”
– Andrew Wartnaby, Owner, Hope Farm, Cato Ridge, KwaZulu-Natal

As dawn breaks over a rustic farm overlooking the rolling hills of the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands in South Africa, a young Burundian woman, Gretta Nyenyeri, sits beside a cooking fire, stirring porridge in a huge steaming pot. The small child tied to her back smiles happily as she waits for her breakfast.
“We are very grateful for what this farmer and his family are doing for us,” she says, “but we know that we can’t stay here for long. We still have nowhere to go, but at least for now we are safe.”
Gretta, her husband Vital, and their little daughter are among the 140 adults and children of Burundian and Congolese origin who came to the aptly named Hope Farm three weeks ago, after South African police forcibly removed them from the site of the last shelter for non-South African refugees displaced by the wave of xenophobic violence that swept through Durban at the beginning of April.
Unable to return to their war-torn home countries like countless others, and afraid to return to the communities that had violently rejected them, they were forced to make a last and desperate stand: with their tents torn down, ablution facilities locked, and prohibited from making fire for cooking or warmth, they had little choice but to sleep out in the open for two nights.
Then, on the morning of Friday 3 July, South African police officers swooped on the site and arrested all of the adults for child neglect and trespassing.
Separated from their children and locked behind bars for the weekend, they were released only when a local farmer – Andrew Wartnaby and his wife Rae – offered to provide them with a fixed address at their farm, a place of refuge while mediation efforts to decide their future got underway.
MSF has been providing medical, psycho-social and advocacy services to the displaced refugees since the early days of the crisis, and is continuing to do so for the ones now staying at Hope Farm.
In contrast to the attacks that drove them to seek shelter in the first place, or the heavy-handed treatment by South African authorities in the months since then, the actions of the Wartnabys have been a bright ray of hope for this group of traumatized people, and for South Africans an example to be admired and perhaps followed.
“When people ask us why we did what we did, my response is, ‘how could we not?’”, says Mr Wartnaby as he sits beside his wife in their farmhouse kitchen later. “The police had separated these people from their kids, and their only crime was that they didn’t have a place to go to.”
Before stepping in to help, the Wartnabys lived a quiet rural life and knew little about the xenophobic attacks and their aftermath. Their farm is totally off the municipal grid, they don’t have a television, and their internet connectivity is patchy at the best of times. But they’re Born Again Christians who have adopted several orphaned children over the past few years, leading to an extended family that comprises all the colours of the rainbow nation, and quite a few dogs and cats.
Rae Wartnaby, a trained nurse, says they’ve been totally overwhelmed by the response to their actions, especially the outpouring of support and assistance from their friends, family, neighbours and total strangers.
“Even the gun-toting farmer down the road stopped by our place during the first week, gave us a thumbs up, and offered to sell us some of his chickens to feed our new guests,” she says.
But the story is far from over.
Just three weeks into this new chapter of the saga, the local police have begun to put pressure on the Wartnabys to evict the displaced people from their farm.
“In the last meeting they gave us until 6 September to get everyone off the farm, or they’re going to charge us with violating municipal bylaws,” says Mr Wartnaby anxiously. “Exactly which ones, they didn’t say.”


Will fill in specific case studies later.

Script:


A PLACE CALLED HOPE

VO: In April, 7 foreign nationals died. Hundreds were injured, and thousands were left displaced.

Forced to flee their homes, thousands of foreign nationals took refuge in temporary camps set up by local municipalities in KZN.

The victims of these attacks were given two options – repatriate or re-integrate.

But that’s easier said than done for many refugees.

VITAL: I could not accept to survive with, for any day any time, I can die and I can loose my life,

VO: Vital Nshimiramana is from Burundi, he has been granted refugee status in South Africa.

He says repatriation is not a viable solution for people from war-torn countries

Also a refugee, Kabange Kaji is from the DRC, she’s fled her country and arrived in South Africa in 2001.

KABANGE: There we ran of safety, we ran of security, we ran of persecution.

VO: Sheena Jonker is from Access to Justice, she works closely with displaced and disadvantaged communities she says Globally, there is a migration crisis.

SHEENA: I think of proportions that we’ve never seen in world history. it really is a crisis. And I think it calls for // NODDY // emergency humanitarian response

LINK: South Africa doesn’t have adequate systems like permanent camps to deal with to deal with refugees, because we have freedom of movement policy – so it seems this is no one’s direct responsibility and there are no obvious solutions.

VO: Because the camps in KwaZulu Natal were never meant to be a permanent fixture, they were shut down after just three months.

Both Kabange and Vital’s families were at the Chatsworth camp in Durban – the last one to be taken down in early July.

VITAL: They took out all the tent // we were sleeping down to the ground // for three days

VO: When the families refused to move, the police were sent in early one Friday morning.

KABANGE: The police and the authorities and the officials were there – they just give us five minutes to pack //
VITAL: They say one, two, three until five and then the commander give them the order//

VO: With nowhere to go, the group of 138 displaced people from the DRC and Burundi were arrested and kept behind bars for the entire weekend.

VITAL: We asked why you locked us, we are refugees, we never steal, we never kill anybody – we are the ones that affected by your community, your people, but now we are punished. They accuse us that we have been abuse our children, by sleeping outside, we abuse our children not buying food for them.

VO: Kabange says she was filled with fear when the police took her children away – all the families were separated.

KABANGE: was very worried, very trauma... very stressful, I was locked, I don’t know where my kids are.

VO: Sheena’s organization stepped in and started consulting with the group in the police cells.

SHEENA: needed to show there was a fixed address for them to go to with their children….

VO: Although the group was suspicious at first, they were desperate to be reunited with their families.

VITAL: even if you are in trouble anyhow. You suffer with your family.

VO: Word spread of group’s plight on social media. After seeing this post on facebook, a KZN Family, the Wartnaby’s, wanted to help.

ANDREW: There was parents and children separated – they had nowhere to stay, and there was nobody else offering assistance.

VO: Despite their eleven biological, adoptive and foster children, cats, dogs and farm animals, Andrew & Rae didn’t hesitate and immediately offered their small holding. The Chatsworth Camp group was released that same day and taken to a place called hope about 40km north of Durban.

RAE: For us it was a simple matter of people who needed some space and some time – they needed to be reunited with their children – which was extremely important to us.
ANDREW: On the way home, I felt sick. I felt absolutely ill, the realisation that no forethought had gone into this. We didn’t have blankets or pillows or food or anywhere for them to sleep.

VO: Support came in quickly from all corners.

ANDREW: IT started with our family, then our neighbours, then organistions, then churches – getting involved and helping.

VO: Relevant stakeholders have set up an ad hoc forum including, the Provincial Departments of Home Affairs, Social Development, the Police, local authorities and community representatives.

But the happy ending was short lived and the trauma was far from over - not everyone is happy about the Wartnaby’s new guests.

RAE: There have been complaints from our neighbours – it did happen suddenly – we did come home one evening with 138 people and obviously there were questions asked and people who felt that there questions haven’t been answered adequately

LINK: Some of the landowners who call themselves the Killarney Valley Landowners say they have empathy for the group, but they also have a long list of concerns.

VO: They have raised questions about the legality and environmental sustainability of such a large group of people moving onto private agricultural land. Claiming that property prices have already started falling.

Simon Steyn represents the landowners.

SIMON: I think if you do something like this and you bring so many people in next to other people, then you need to consider them and how it will impact their lives

VO: They feel while the Wartnaby’s guests are impacting negatively on the area and dividing the community, there doesn’t seem to be a plan of action to address their concerns.

SIMON: This could drag out for quite a long time, because when I asked them have you got any firm plans in place and the answer was no….expected a some kind of plan after a month.

VO The landowners have taken their complaints to the Mkhambathini Municipality, formerly Camperdown - they are taking these concerns seriously.

ANDREW: The municipality have been very concerned about increased water usage, increased burden on their resources and definitely across the board it’s been how long is going to be, what’s the date, when does it end? INT6 M3

VO: The Wartnaby’s have been given until the first week of September to get rid of their guests.

Mayor Thobekile Maphumulo says they have an obligation to the greater community.

DEREK: washing hands
MAYOR: We are not against the refugees in our area,// but we are going to implement the rules and regulations of this municipality as it is.

VO: According to local authorities, Hope Farm is currently in contravention of the Spatial Land Use Act – the municipality is not happy – if the deadline isn’t met, there will be consequences.

MAYOR: what we are going to do is just to say impose the spot fine of R7500 to the owner of the farm and then the R750 on daily basis

VO: But following the letter of the law, issuing deadlines and fines won’t solve the plight of the Hope Farm foreign nationals. Many, who like Kabange fled their own countries during civil unrest and genocide, feel they have nowhere to turn.

KABANGE: We are are like people who are homeless, we are like people in the street, we don’t have a place to go. We like, I don’t know, like orphan. INT1 M13

VO: A sentiment shared by Vital – he fled Burundi as young boy at the height of genocide. His father a Hutu and mother a Tutsi – they had escaped many attacks until a fateful day that would change everything.

VITAL: We could not knowing it was going to happen,// my father they assassinated him in my eyes it is not easy to survive with people you saw, you knows, it’s not easy

VO: South Africa was a beacon of light for many refugees fleeing persecution.

KABANGE: // we know here in South Africa they respect human rights // but to our surprised, the South Africa that we knew was going to be our – home, that we are going to be safe // the same thing that happened to my country that same thing will happen to me again here, not once, twice! INT 1 M10

VO: When the 2008 xenophobic attacks flared up across South Africa, tens of thousands of foreign nationals were displaced, and more than 60 people lost their lives.

SHEENA: It’s the armchair anti-xenophobic approach lacks the substance of insightful enquiry into the situation our own poor are actually dealing with.

VO: But for Vital, it’s simply an irrational hatred for foreigners. He was violently attacked in 2008, by a group of Zulu speaking locals.

VITAL: I am not a good speaker about that language. Then they started to hit me till I fell down, they hit me on the head, until I loose my conscious. I was almost dead that day. INT 2 M4

VO: Kabange’s son was severely beaten in this year’s April attacks.

KABANGE: I can’t continue staying in South Africa – because I am scared, I fear of my life – I don’t know what will happen next.

VO: It’s an unprecedented situation in South Africa that is extremely complex says United Nations Senior Field Co-oridinator Acacio Juliao.

ACCASSIO: there is no quick fix, if the idea is to go outside of SA.

VO: This responsibility falls on the UN Human Rights Commission – but it’s an intensive process says Acacio.

ACASSIO: One of the key elements is a country willing to receive the displaced people, the refugees for that matter. // it can take up to 2-3 years,

VO: Time, the Hope Farm Group doesn’t have with the municipality’s deadline looming.

DEREK: would you do it again?
RAE: Absolutely
ANDREW: Without a doubt. This was a specific response to a specific incident // There’s no way I would have been able to walk away //I firmly believe that if you are able to help, you should.
VITAL: There are somethings as a Christian you can’t change, you can’t bring back – but you have to have hope.




PROMOS

Not sure which of these are 10 and which are 15?

PROMO 1
VO: A selfless KZN family takes in 138 desperate refugees displaced by xenophobic violence only to face the wrath of local government

ANDREW: “There is no way i would be able to walk away – if you can help you should”

PROMO 2
VO: A selfless KZN family gives refuge to a 138 foreigners traumatised by April’s xenophobic violence. But the KZN authorities won’t let them stay.

KABANGE: We are are like people who are homeless, we are like people in the street, we don’t have a place to go. We like, I don’t know, like orphan. INT1 M13

PROMO 3

VO: A Place Called Hope, the last safe haven for foreign nationals displaced by xenophobic violence in KZN is now also under threat.

KABANGE: We don’t have a place to go. We like, I don’t know, like orphan.

VO: Carte Blanche asks where to next?

VITAL: We could not knowing it was going to happen,// my father they assassinated him in my eyes it is not easy to survive with people you saw, you knows, it’s not easy VO: South Africa was a beacon of light for many refugees fleeing persecution. KABANGE: // we know here in South Africa they respect human rights // but to our surprised, the South Africa that we knew was going to be our – home, that we are going to be safe // the same thing that happened to my country that same thing will happen to me again here, not once, twice! INT 1 M10 VO: When the 2008 xenophobic attacks flared up across South Africa, tens of thousands of foreign nationals were displaced, and more than 60 people lost their lives. SHEENA: It’s the armchair anti-xenophobic approach lacks the substance of insightful enquiry into the situation our own poor are actually dealing with. VO: But for Vital, it’s simply an irrational hatred for foreigners. He was violently attacked in 2008, by a group of Zulu speaking locals. VITAL: I am not a good speaker about that language. Then they started to hit me till I fell down, they hit me on the head, until I loose my conscious. I was almost dead that day. INT 2 M4 VO: Kabange’s son was severely beaten in this year’s April attacks. KABANGE: I can’t continue staying in South Africa – because I am scared, I fear of my life – I don’t know what will happen next. VO: It’s an unprecedented situation in South Africa that is extremely complex says United Nations Senior Field Co-oridinator Acacio Juliao. ACCASSIO: there is no quick fix, if the idea is to go outside of SA. VO: This responsibility falls on the UN Human Rights Commission – but it’s an intensive process says Acacio. ACASSIO: One of the key elements is a country willing to receive the displaced people, the refugees for that matter. // it can take up to 2-3 years, VO: Time, the Hope Farm Group doesn’t have with the municipality’s deadline looming. DEREK: would you do it again? RAE: Absolutely ANDREW: Without a doubt. This was a specific response to a specific incident // There’s no way I would have been able to walk away //I firmly believe that if you are able to help, you should. VITAL: There are somethings as a Christian you can’t change, you can’t bring back – but you have to have hope. PROMOS Not sure which of these are 10 and which are 15? metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): a Place Called Hope, the last safe haven for foreign nationals affected by xenophobia now also under threat.
metadata.Summary: When xenophobic attacks flared up in April in parts of KZN thousand of foreign nationals were displaced. Many to shelter in temporary refugee camps set up local municipalities. But three months later, those camps would be torn down leaving many of the foreigners displaced again. A family in Camperdown opened their doors, welcoming the refugees to Hope Farm. But just one month later, the owners are now being threatened with legal action against them if they do not remove the people from their privately owned farm. We bring you the stories of a community desperate for a place to call home, a family that wanted to help and municipality that is out to get them.
metadata.Further information: “When people ask us why we did what we did, my response is: ‘How could we not?’” – Andrew Wartnaby, Owner, Hope Farm, Cato Ridge, KwaZulu-Natal As dawn breaks over a rustic farm overlooking the rolling hills of the KwaZulu-Natal Midlands in South Africa, a young Burundian woman, Gretta Nyenyeri, sits beside a cooking fire, stirring porridge in a huge steaming pot. The small child tied to her back smiles happily as she waits for her breakfast. “We are very grateful for what this farmer and his family are doing for us,” she says, “but we know that we can’t stay here for long. We still have nowhere to go, but at least for now we are safe.” Gretta, her husband Vital, and their little daughter are among the 140 adults and children of Burundian and Congolese origin who came to the aptly named Hope Farm three weeks ago, after South African police forcibly removed them from the site of the last shelter for non-South African refugees displaced by the wave of xenophobic violence that swept through Durban at the beginning of April. Unable to return to their war-torn home countries like countless others, and afraid to return to the communities that had violently rejected them, they were forced to make a last and desperate stand: with their tents torn down, ablution facilities locked, and prohibited from making fire for cooking or warmth, they had little choice but to sleep out in the open for two nights. Then, on the morning of Friday 3 July, South African police officers swooped on the site and arrested all of the adults for child neglect and trespassing. Separated from their children and locked behind bars for the weekend, they were released only when a local farmer – Andrew Wartnaby and his wife Rae – offered to provide them with a fixed address at their farm, a place of refuge while mediation efforts to decide their future got underway. MSF has been providing medical, psycho-social and advocacy services to the displaced refugees since the early days of the crisis, and is continuing to do so for the ones now staying at Hope Farm. In contrast to the attacks that drove them to seek shelter in the first place, or the heavy-handed treatment by South African authorities in the months since then, the actions of the Wartnabys have been a bright ray of hope for this group of traumatized people, and for South Africans an example to be admired and perhaps followed. “When people ask us why we did what we did, my response is, ‘how could we not?’”, says Mr Wartnaby as he sits beside his wife in their farmhouse kitchen later. “The police had separated these people from their kids, and their only crime was that they didn’t have a place to go to.” Before stepping in to help, the Wartnabys lived a quiet rural life and knew little about the xenophobic attacks and their aftermath. Their farm is totally off the municipal grid, they don’t have a television, and their internet connectivity is patchy at the best of times. But they’re Born Again Christians who have adopted several orphaned children over the past few years, leading to an extended family that comprises all the colours of the rainbow nation, and quite a few dogs and cats. Rae Wartnaby, a trained nurse, says they’ve been totally overwhelmed by the response to their actions, especially the outpouring of support and assistance from their friends, family, neighbours and total strangers. “Even the gun-toting farmer down the road stopped by our place during the first week, gave us a thumbs up, and offered to sell us some of his chickens to feed our new guests,” she says. But the story is far from over. Just three weeks into this new chapter of the saga, the local police have begun to put pressure on the Wartnabys to evict the displaced people from their farm. “In the last meeting they gave us until 6 September to get everyone off the farm, or they’re going to charge us with violating municipal bylaws,” says Mr Wartnaby anxiously. “Exactly which ones, they didn’t say.” Will fill in specific case studies later.
